title: Grignard + ketone → 3° alcohol

steps.label: The Grignard's C–Mg electrons attack the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: The C–Mg bond is polarized C(δ−)–Mg(δ+), so the carbon acts like a carbanion.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: H3O+ is added only after the Grignard is used up: acid would destroy the Grignard reagent.

why: The C=O carbon is electrophilic and the Grignard carbon is a strong carbon nucleophile. A ketone has no leaving group, so the methyl just adds; acid workup then protonates the alkoxide.

traps.explains: That's what a hydride (NaBH4) gives. A Grignard delivers a carbon, so a new C–C bond forms.
The Grignard carbon bonds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not to the oxygen. No ether forms.
Mild aqueous acid workup only protonates the alkoxide. Dehydrating the alcohol to an alkene would need heat and strong acid.

distractors.explains: An alcohol's O–H is acidic enough to destroy a Grignard (it just protonates it to methane). Grignards need a C=O to add to.
NaBH4 adds hydride, not carbon, so this gives 2-propanol. The target has a new C–C bond.

title: NaBH4 + aldehyde → 1° alcohol

steps.label: Hydride from NaBH4 attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: The real hydride donor is the B–H bond of BH4⁻; it is drawn here as H⁻.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: In practice the methanol solvent often supplies this proton before workup.

why: NaBH4 is a source of hydride (H⁻), a nucleophile that adds to the electrophilic C=O carbon. An aldehyde has no leaving group, so H just adds; protonating the alkoxide gives a 1° alcohol.

traps.explains: NaBH4 is a reducing agent: it adds H to the carbonyl. Getting a carboxylic acid would need an oxidant (e.g. H2CrO4).
NaBH4 stops at the alcohol. Removing the oxygen completely (C=O → CH2) needs Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen conditions.
Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon (C1) and the skeleton doesn't change, so the OH stays on C1. An aldehyde gives a 1° alcohol; only a ketone gives a 2° one.

title: NaBH4 + ketone → 2° alcohol

steps.label: Hydride from NaBH4 attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: The real hydride donor is the B–H bond of BH4⁻; it is drawn here as H⁻.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: In practice the methanol solvent often supplies this proton before workup.

why: Hydride from NaBH4 adds to the electrophilic C=O carbon and the π electrons go to oxygen. A ketone has no leaving group, so the alkoxide just gets protonated, giving a 2° alcohol.

traps.explains: NaBH4 stops at the alcohol. Turning C=O all the way into CH2 needs Wolff–Kishner (H2NNH2, KOH, heat) or Clemmensen (Zn(Hg), HCl).
Workup only protonates the alkoxide. Dehydrating the alcohol to an alkene would need strong acid and heat.
Methanol is just the solvent and proton source. The new bond to the carbonyl carbon is to H (from BH4⁻), not to OCH3.

title: LiAlH4 + ketone → 2° alcohol

steps.label: Hydride from LiAlH4 attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: Hydride can attack either face of the flat C=O, so the new stereocenter forms as a racemic mixture.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: LiAlH4 reacts violently with water, so the proton source is added only in a separate workup step.

why: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the electrophilic C=O carbon, giving an alkoxide. LiAlH4 reacts violently with water and alcohols, so it is used in dry ether first and the alkoxide is protonated in a separate H3O+ workup step.

traps.explains: LiAlH4 reduces a ketone only as far as the alcohol. Removing the O completely (C=O → CH2) is Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen.
Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon (C2) and the skeleton doesn't move, so the OH stays on C2: a 2° alcohol, not 1-butanol.
The H3O+ workup is mild and only protonates the alkoxide. Dehydration to an alkene needs strong acid and heat.

title: Grignard + formaldehyde → 1° alcohol (one more carbon)

steps.label: The ethyl carbon of the Grignard attacks the formaldehyde carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: Formaldehyde has no carbon groups on C=O, so the product is a 1° alcohol with one more carbon.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+

why: The Grignard carbon is a strong carbon nucleophile and attacks the electrophilic C=O carbon of formaldehyde. Formaldehyde's carbon carries two H's, so after acid workup it becomes a CH2OH: a 1° alcohol with one more carbon than the Grignard.

traps.explains: Formaldehyde's carbon has two H's, so after the ethyl adds it is bonded to only one carbon: a 1° alcohol. A 2° alcohol needs an aldehyde like acetaldehyde.
Workup just protonates the alkoxide. Nothing oxidizes it to an aldehyde.
The Grignard carbon bonds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not to oxygen. No ether forms.

distractors.explains: Methyl adds to acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, which already has a CH3, so this gives 2-propanol (a 2° alcohol), not 1-propanol.
Ethanol has no C=O to add to. Its O–H simply protonates the Grignard (giving methane), so no C–C bond forms.

title: Grignard + aldehyde → 2° alcohol

steps.label: The Grignard's methyl carbon attacks the aldehyde carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: An aldehyde carbon carries one H and one R group, so adding a second R gives a 2° alcohol.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+

why: The Grignard carbon attacks the electrophilic aldehyde carbon, and the C=O π electrons go to oxygen. An aldehyde carbon already has one carbon group and one H, so adding a second carbon group gives a 2° alcohol after acid workup.

traps.explains: That's what NaBH4 gives (hydride adds). A Grignard delivers a carbon, so the product gains a CH3.
The alkoxide is simply protonated on workup. Nothing oxidizes it to a ketone, and an aldehyde has no leaving group to lose.
Mild acid workup only protonates the alkoxide. Dehydrating to an alkene needs strong acid and heat.

distractors.explains: Adding methyl to a ketone gives a 3° alcohol (2-methyl-2-butanol), not the 2° alcohol 2-butanol.
NaBH4 adds hydride, not carbon, so propanal becomes 1-propanol. The target has an extra carbon and a new C–C bond.

title: Acetylide + ketone → propargylic 3° alcohol

steps.label: The acetylide carbon's lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: The new C–C bond is to the carbon that carried the negative charge, so the triple bond stays intact.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide oxygen takes a proton from H3O+

why: The acetylide carbon carries a negative charge, so it is a good carbon nucleophile, and it adds to the electrophilic C=O carbon of acetone. A ketone has no leaving group, so it just adds; H3O+ workup protonates the alkoxide to give a 3° alcohol that keeps the triple bond.

traps.explains: Nothing in this reaction reduces the triple bond. Making the alkene would need a separate step such as H2 with Lindlar's catalyst.
The nucleophilic atom is the acetylide carbon, and it bonds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, not to oxygen.
HC≡C⁻ has only one negative carbon. The other end still has its H, so with one deprotonation only one acetone adds.

distractors.explains: Acetaldehyde has only one methyl on its carbonyl carbon, so this gives 3-butyn-2-ol (a 2° alcohol), one CH3 short of the target.
Acetylide is a strong base, so on a 2° halide it mostly eliminates (propene). Even SN2 would give an alkyne with no OH.

title: Cyanohydrin formation: HCN adds to C=O

steps.label: Cyanide's carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: Cyanide attacks through carbon (the negatively charged atom), forming a new C–C bond.

steps.label: The alkoxide takes a proton from HCN, regenerating cyanide
steps.note: This step makes a new CN⁻, which is why only a catalytic amount of NaCN is needed.

why: Cyanide's carbon is the nucleophile and attacks the electrophilic C=O carbon. The alkoxide is then protonated by HCN (which regenerates cyanide), giving a cyanohydrin: OH and CN on the same carbon.

traps.explains: A ketone has no leaving group, so cyanide adds; it doesn't replace the oxygen. Swapping a group for CN is SN2 on an alkyl halide.
The nitrile survives these conditions. Hydrolyzing it to an α-hydroxy acid is a separate step with hot aqueous acid.
Nothing here dehydrates the cyanohydrin. The OH stays; losing water to make the alkene would need much harsher conditions.

distractors.explains: SN2 swaps Br for CN, giving 2-methylpropanenitrile with no OH (and a 2° halide also eliminates). The OH of a cyanohydrin comes from a C=O oxygen.
2-Propanol has no C=O for cyanide to add to, and OH⁻ is a poor leaving group, so nothing happens.

title: Hydrate formation: water adds to C=O

steps.label: The carbonyl oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: Protonation makes the carbonyl carbon much more electrophilic, so even weak nucleophiles like water can add.

steps.label: Water attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Water removes a proton from the oxonium ion, giving the hydrate and regenerating H3O+
steps.note: The acid is regenerated, so it is a catalyst. Every step is reversible.

why: Water is a weak nucleophile, so acid helps by protonating the C=O and making the carbon more electrophilic. Water adds, a proton is lost, and the product is a gem-diol (hydrate). Formaldehyde has no carbon groups to stabilize the C=O, so the equilibrium lies almost fully on the hydrate side.

traps.explains: Water adds across the C=O; nothing is oxidized. The hydrate carbon is at the same oxidation level as the aldehyde.
Water isn't a hydride source, so nothing is reduced. You'd need NaBH4 or LiAlH4 to get methanol.
That's an acetal, which forms with an alcohol (2 CH3OH, H+). With water as the nucleophile you get the gem-diol.

title: Acetal formation: ketone + 2 CH3OH, H+

steps.label: The carbonyl oxygen takes a proton from protonated methanol (the acid catalyst)
steps.note: In methanol, the strongest acid present is CH3OH2+.

steps.label: Methanol attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Methanol removes the proton from the oxonium ion, giving the hemiacetal
steps.note: The hemiacetal (one OH, one OCH3 on the same carbon) is the halfway point.

steps.label: The OH group takes a proton, turning it into a good leaving group
steps.note: OH⁻ is a poor leaving group; water is a good one.

steps.label: Water leaves, pushed out by a lone pair on the OCH3 oxygen, giving an oxocarbenium ion
steps.note: Removing this water (Dean–Stark trap or drying agent) drives the equilibrium toward the acetal.

steps.label: A second methanol attacks the oxocarbenium carbon
Methanol removes the last proton, giving the acetal and regenerating the acid catalyst

why: Acid makes the C=O carbon electrophilic, methanol adds to give a hemiacetal, and acid turns its OH into water, a good leaving group. Losing water gives an oxocarbenium ion, which a second methanol attacks. Removing water drives the equilibrium to the acetal.

traps.explains: That's the hemiacetal, an intermediate. With acid and excess methanol its OH is protonated, leaves as water, and a second CH3OH adds.
That's the hydrate, which forms with water. Here methanol is the nucleophile and water is removed.
Nothing reduces the carbon. The old carbonyl carbon ends up with two C–O bonds (two OCH3 groups), not one O and one H.

title: Cyclic acetal with ethylene glycol (protecting group)

steps.label: The carbonyl oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
One OH of ethylene glycol attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon
Water removes the proton from the oxonium ion, giving the hemiacetal
The OH group takes a proton, turning it into a good leaving group
Water leaves, pushed out by a lone pair on the ring-to-be oxygen, giving an oxocarbenium ion
The second OH of the same glycol attacks the oxocarbenium carbon, closing a 5-membered ring
steps.note: Because the second OH is on the same molecule, this ring closure is fast and entropically favoured.

steps.label: Water removes the last proton, giving the cyclic acetal and regenerating H3O+

why: It's acetal formation with both OH groups on one molecule: one OH adds, water leaves, and the second OH closes a five-membered ring on the oxocarbenium ion. The cyclic acetal is unreactive toward bases, Grignards and hydrides, so it protects a ketone; H3O+ removes it later.

traps.explains: That's the hemiacetal, an intermediate. Acid turns its OH into water, which leaves, and the glycol's second OH closes the ring.
One glycol supplies both oxygens. Its second OH is right there, so closing the five-membered ring is much faster than bringing in another glycol molecule.
Nothing reduces the carbon. The old carbonyl carbon ends up with two C–O bonds, both to the glycol.

title: Acetal hydrolysis: H3O+ gives back the ketone

steps.label: One OCH3 oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
steps.note: Acetals are stable to base; they only fall apart once acid makes the OR group leavable.

steps.label: Methanol leaves, pushed out by a lone pair on the other OCH3, giving an oxocarbenium ion
Water attacks the oxocarbenium carbon
steps.note: Excess water pushes every equilibrium toward hydrolysis: the acetal mechanism run backward.

steps.label: Water removes a proton from the oxonium ion, giving the hemiacetal
The remaining OCH3 oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
Methanol leaves, pushed out by a lone pair on the OH oxygen, giving the protonated ketone
Water removes the proton from oxygen, giving the ketone and regenerating H3O+

why: Acetal formation run backwards: acid protonates one OCH3 so methanol can leave, giving an oxocarbenium ion that water attacks. Repeating this loses the second methanol, and with lots of water the equilibrium goes back to the ketone.

traps.explains: That's the hemiacetal, an intermediate. In excess aqueous acid it loses the second methanol and goes on to the ketone.
Acetone's hydrate is only a tiny fraction at equilibrium. The product you isolate is the ketone.
Water and acid don't reduce anything. The carbon keeps two bonds to oxygen, as a C=O.

title: Imine formation: ketone + 1° amine

steps.label: The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: Mild acid (pH about 4–5) is best: enough to help later steps, not so much that all the amine is protonated.

steps.label: The negatively charged oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
Water removes a proton from the nitrogen, giving the carbinolamine
steps.note: The carbinolamine (OH and N on the same carbon) is the tetrahedral intermediate.

steps.label: The OH group takes a proton, turning it into a good leaving group
Water leaves, pushed out by the nitrogen lone pair, giving an iminium ion
Water removes the proton from nitrogen, giving the imine
steps.note: A 1° amine still has an N–H on the iminium, so the proton comes off nitrogen and C=N remains.

why: The amine's nitrogen lone pair attacks the electrophilic C=O carbon to give a carbinolamine. Mild acid turns the OH into water, which leaves, and because a 1° amine's N still has an H to lose, a C=N double bond (imine) forms.

traps.explains: That's the enamine tautomer. With a 1° amine the N can lose its own H, so the C=N imine forms. Enamines come from 2° amines.
That's the carbinolamine intermediate. Acid catalysis lets the OH leave as water, so it goes on to the C=N.
That amine is the reductive amination product; it needs a reducing agent such as NaBH3CN. Without one, you stop at the C=N.

title: Enamine formation: ketone + 2° amine

steps.label: The pyrrolidine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
The negatively charged oxygen takes a proton from H3O+
Water removes the proton from nitrogen, giving the carbinolamine
The OH group takes a proton, turning it into a good leaving group
Water leaves, pushed out by the nitrogen lone pair, giving an iminium ion
Water removes a proton from the α-carbon; the C=N π electrons move onto nitrogen, giving the enamine
steps.note: This iminium has no N–H (2° amine), so the proton has to come from the α-carbon instead: C=C–N, not C=N.

why: The nitrogen of pyrrolidine attacks the C=O carbon, and acid helps water leave to give an iminium ion. A 2° amine's N has no H left to lose, so a proton is removed from the α-carbon instead, forming a C=C next to N: an enamine.

traps.explains: That iminium ion is an intermediate. The N has no H to lose, so it can't become a neutral imine; instead an α-H is removed to give the enamine.
That's the carbinolamine intermediate. Acid catalysis lets the OH leave as water, so the reaction keeps going.
The C=C forms between the old carbonyl carbon and its α-carbon, so N sits directly on the alkene carbon, not one carbon away.

title: Wittig: ketone + Ph3P=CH2 → alkene

steps.label: The ylide's negatively charged carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon
steps.note: The ylide is a carbanion next to P+; written as Ph3P=CH2 it is the same molecule.

steps.label: The alkoxide oxygen bonds to phosphorus, closing a 4-membered oxaphosphetane ring
The ring breaks apart: C=C forms and P=O forms
steps.note: The very strong P=O bond in triphenylphosphine oxide is the driving force.

why: The ylide's negative carbon attacks the C=O carbon. The oxygen then bonds to phosphorus (oxaphosphetane), and the ring falls apart into the very stable Ph3P=O and a new C=C exactly where the C=O was.

traps.explains: That's the alcohol a Grignard (CH3MgBr) gives. With an ylide, the oxygen ends up on phosphorus as Ph3P=O, leaving a C=C.
The Wittig puts the C=C exactly where the C=O was (here outside the ring). It doesn't move to the more substituted position like an E1 dehydration would.
Nothing adds H2. The new C=C between the ring carbon and CH2 is still there in the product.

distractors.explains: Acid dehydration goes through a carbocation and gives mostly the more substituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev), not the exocyclic C=CH2.
The Grignard adds and stops: workup gives the alcohol 1-methylcyclohexanol, not an alkene.

review: Mechanism drawn the Wade/McMurry way (ylide C attacks C=O → betaine-type alkoxide → oxaphosphetane). Current evidence for unstabilized ylides favours direct [2+2] oxaphosphetane formation; some courses (e.g. newer Klein) draw it that way.

title: Wolff–Kishner: C=O → CH2

steps.label: A hydrazine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen
steps.note: Steps 1–5 make the hydrazone, the same way an imine forms.

steps.label: The negatively charged oxygen takes a proton from water
Hydroxide removes a proton from the positively charged nitrogen
Hydroxide leaves, pushed out by the nitrogen lone pair
Hydroxide removes the proton from nitrogen, giving the hydrazone
Hydroxide removes a proton from the terminal NH2
steps.note: Strong base and heat (about 200 °C in a high-boiling solvent) are what make these N–H steps go.

steps.label: The anion is protonated on carbon by water (through its resonance form)
steps.note: The former carbonyl carbon now has its first new C–H bond.

steps.label: Hydroxide removes the second N–H proton
N2 leaves, giving a carbanion
steps.note: Loss of N2 gas is irreversible and pulls the whole reaction forward.

steps.label: The carbanion takes a proton from water, giving the CH2 group

why: Hydrazine's nitrogen attacks the C=O carbon and water is lost, giving a hydrazone (like imine formation). Strong base and heat then remove the N–H protons, N2 gas leaves, and the carbon picks up a second H, so the C=O becomes CH2.

traps.explains: That's the alcohol NaBH4 or LiAlH4 would give. Wolff–Kishner removes the oxygen completely: C=O becomes CH2.
The hydrazone is the intermediate. KOH and heat drive off N2, so it goes all the way to the CH2.
Only the C=O is reduced. The benzene ring stays aromatic.

title: Clemmensen: C=O → CH2 in acid
why: Zinc amalgam in hot HCl removes the carbonyl oxygen completely, turning C=O into CH2. Acid activates the C=O (protonation), and electrons from the zinc surface reduce the carbon. It is the acidic partner of Wolff–Kishner: use it when the molecule can survive strong acid but not strong base.

traps.explains: That's the alcohol a hydride (NaBH4/LiAlH4) gives. Clemmensen removes the oxygen completely: C=O becomes CH2.
HCl here is the acid for the reduction; the product doesn't keep a C–Cl bond. The carbon ends up as a plain CH2.
Only the C=O is reduced. The benzene ring stays aromatic.
